architectural_implications.after: The model writes Python/bash against an SDK; capability is composed at execution time inside the sandbox.
architectural_implications.before: Integrations are registered as individual tools with JSON schemas and dispatched by the model's tool-choice.
architectural_implications.consequence: Tool-schema token overhead disappears and the action space becomes composable, but the system now needs code sandboxing, egress control, and error surfaces that were previously handled by tool handlers.
architectural_implications.observation: The action interface moves from an enumerated tool registry to a programmatic SDK executed in a sandbox.

architectural_implications.after: Intermediate results are written to files and referenced by path, re-read on demand.
architectural_implications.before: Intermediate results are accumulated in the message history and re-sent each turn.
architectural_implications.consequence: Per-step token cost becomes roughly flat in run length; the new cost is I/O and the need for agents to manage their own working set, which must be instructed explicitly (e.g., via AGENTS.md).
architectural_implications.observation: Agent state migrates from the context window to the filesystem.

architectural_implications.after: Queue schedules steps, workers execute them, an append-only event store records them and enables replay from checkpoint.
architectural_implications.before: A single long-lived process holds the loop; a crash, rollout, or client disconnect destroys the run.
architectural_implications.consequence: Runs become resumable and auditable, and time-travel debugging becomes possible, at the cost of operating a stateful backend and defining an event schema that must stay replay-compatible.
architectural_implications.observation: The agent loop is extracted from the request lifecycle into a durable control plane.

architectural_implications.after: A proxy holds secrets; the sandbox only reaches allowlisted domains.
architectural_implications.before: Secrets are available to the process (environment variables or config) that performs the action.
architectural_implications.consequence: Compromise of the sandbox no longer implies credential compromise, but every external dependency must be reached through the proxy and allowlist, adding an integration and configuration surface.
architectural_implications.observation: Credential handling is pushed out of the execution environment.

article_ideas.angle: Frame tool calling as a per-turn contract paid in tokens, quantify what that contract buys and costs as N grows, then show that the migration is not a free win — it trades a bounded tool list for arbitrary execution capability that must be constrained elsewhere.
article_ideas.audience: Agent platform engineers and technical leads choosing between tool registries and code-execution harnesses
article_ideas.based_on: turns an N-tool selection problem into a code-writing problem
article_ideas.thesis: Enumerating integrations as JSON tools charges a fixed schema tax on every model call and converts a composition problem into a selection problem; when the action space is wide and sparse, exposing an SDK plus a language raises both the cost ceiling and the accuracy ceiling, at the price of moving safety from the tool permission layer to the sandbox and network layer.
article_ideas.title: Your Tool Menu Is a Token Tax: Why Wide, Sparse Action Spaces Should Be Programs, Not Schemas

article_ideas.angle: Treat the context window as a register file rather than a database, derive the superlinear cost of naive accumulation, then present externalize/checkpoint/re-read as cost engineering with its own failure mode (stale or misreferenced files) instead of prompt tuning.
article_ideas.audience: Engineers operating production agents and platform owners accountable for inference spend
article_ideas.based_on: every step re-sends the accumulated context, so cost grows superlinearly with run length
article_ideas.thesis: The binding constraint on multi-hour agent runs is not model capability but the cost curve of monotonically re-sent context; making context size roughly constant in step count by spilling state to an addressable filesystem is the design change that makes long runs viable, and it must be instructed explicitly rather than assumed.
article_ideas.title: Long-Running Agents Fail Economically Before They Fail Technically

article_ideas.angle: Recount the failure causes (worker evictions, rollouts, client disconnects) that in-process loops cannot survive, describe the control-plane decomposition, then stress-test the deterministic-replay claim rather than accepting it.
article_ideas.audience: Backend and infrastructure engineers building agent runtimes
article_ideas.based_on: relocates durability responsibility from the model loop (which cannot be trusted to survive) to the backend
article_ideas.thesis: A single long-lived process holding the agent loop is the wrong durability boundary; modelling each step as an event in a queue/worker/append-only store makes runs resumable and auditable, but the reward is bounded by how deterministic replay actually is once model sampling and external side effects are in the log.
article_ideas.title: Move the Loop Out of the Request: Agent Durability Is a Control-Plane Problem

connections.relationship: Substitutes an addressable external store for the prompt as the location of working state, converting superlinear context cost into roughly constant per-step cost.
Reapplies classical append-only-log and replay patterns from backend engineering to the agent control plane.
Both are consequences of granting arbitrary code execution: security must be enforced at the network and credential boundary rather than at a tool-permission boundary.
Self-repair at L4 requires the agent to read execution logs, which makes observability data a first-class input to the loop rather than a human-only artifact.
A versioned environment template is a precondition for replaying an event log faithfully, since execution depends on the environment as much as on the recorded steps.

evidence_quotes.text: Tool calling is a contract on tokens (JSON schemas).
Giving an LLM 20+ tools creates noise and wastes tokens when only 1 tool is needed.
Benchmarks from Vercel, Anthropic, Cloudflare, and Microsoft showing token reduction up to 99.9% and accuracy increases.

core_insights.generalization: Any agent surface where the action space is wide and sparse (few actions used per turn) should be exposed as a programmable API rather than enumerated as discrete tools; the wider and sparser the action space, the larger the win.
core_insights.insight: Replacing a large tool menu with a general code-execution interface (Python/bash plus an SDK) collapses the per-turn token cost of tool schemas and removes the classifier/selection bottleneck, because the model expresses intent in code rather than choosing among 20+ JSON contracts.
core_insights.why_it_matters: Tool definitions are a fixed tax paid on every model call; at 20+ tools the schema payload dominates the prompt and creates selection noise. Moving the interface to a language plus SDK turns an N-tool selection problem into a code-writing problem, which changes both cost structure and accuracy ceiling for long-running agents.

evidence_quotes.text: Filesystem acts as the agent's extended context, reducing payload size in the context window.
Instruct agents via AGENTS.md to write intermediate results to files and re-read on demand.

core_insights.generalization: Treat the context window as a register file, not a database: any artifact larger than the reasoning needs should be spilled to an addressable store and re-read on demand. This applies to any long-horizon agent, not just coding agents.
core_insights.insight: The sandbox filesystem is treated as the agent's extended context: intermediate payloads are written to disk and referenced by path instead of being carried in the context window.
core_insights.why_it_matters: It moves state out of the most expensive and least controllable storage (the prompt) into a persistent, addressable store, which simultaneously cuts token spend, avoids polluting context with garbage intermediate data, and gives the run durable state that survives process death.

evidence_quotes.text: Event sourcing (queue, worker, event store) enables crash recovery, time-travel debugging, audit trails, and deterministic replay.
Processes die due to worker evictions, rollouts, or client disconnects.
Implement queue-worker-eventstore architectures for any agent run lasting longer than a few minutes.

core_insights.generalization: Any agent run measured in minutes-to-hours should be modeled as a durable workflow whose steps are events, not as a single long-lived process; the longer the run, the more the value shifts from prompt engineering to control-plane engineering.
core_insights.insight: Agent step execution is decomposed into queue / worker / append-only event store, applying classical event sourcing to the agent loop so runs survive worker evictions, rollouts, and client disconnects and can be replayed from a checkpoint.
core_insights.why_it_matters: It relocates durability responsibility from the model loop (which cannot be trusted to survive) to the backend, and unlocks capabilities the in-process loop cannot offer: crash recovery, deterministic replay, time-travel debugging, and audit trails.

evidence_quotes.text: Combines a model-execution loop with limited tool primitives in an isolated sandbox environment backed by a template.
Codex CLI, Claude Code, and OpenCode CLI utilizing shell, read, write, and edit primitives.

core_insights.generalization: Design agent capability as (small primitive set) x (general-purpose runtime) x (reproducible environment template) rather than as a growing integration list; the template becomes the unit of versioning and reproducibility.
core_insights.insight: The harness is defined as a four-part boundary — model+loop, a deliberately small set of primitives (files, bash, python), an isolated sandbox (filesystem, execution, outbound network), and a sandbox template — rather than an unbounded tool registry.
core_insights.why_it_matters: It gives a concrete decomposition for where responsibilities live: capability comes from the sandbox and primitives, not from enumerating integrations. This makes the system reproducible (template) and the capability set stable while the reachable action space stays effectively unbounded via code.

evidence_quotes.text: Network access must be strictly controlled with allowlisted domains and proxies for secrets.

core_insights.generalization: When the agent can run arbitrary code, permissioning must move from the action layer to the network and credential layer; assume anything inside the sandbox is readable by an adversary-influenced process.
core_insights.insight: Sandbox egress is a first-class security boundary: network access is limited to allowlisted domains and secrets are injected via proxy rather than placed in the sandbox.
core_insights.why_it_matters: Code-executing agents have arbitrary outbound capability, so the blast radius is determined by network policy and credential handling, not by tool permissions. Proxying secrets keeps credentials out of the filesystem that the agent (and anything it downloads) can read.

evidence_quotes.text: Context grows every step, making re-sending the full context increasingly expensive.

core_insights.generalization: For any agent with step count N, total token cost scales with the integral of context size; the design goal is to make context size roughly constant in N by spilling state to external stores.
core_insights.insight: Monotonically growing context is framed as an economic failure mode of long runs: every step re-sends the accumulated context, so cost grows superlinearly with run length unless state is externalized and checkpointed.
core_insights.why_it_matters: It explains why long-running agents fail economically before they fail technically, and it makes context management a cost-engineering discipline (externalize, checkpoint, re-read) rather than a prompt-tuning one.

evidence_quotes.text: L4 is autonomous operators observing logs and fixing errors.
L5 is autonomous organization (acting like a CEO).

core_insights.generalization: The required reliability, observability, and durability stack should be derived from the autonomy level targeted, not adopted wholesale from the most advanced reference architecture.
core_insights.insight: Agent autonomy is stratified L0–L5 (manual → text generation → accept/decline copilot → goal-based delegated agent → autonomous operator observing logs and fixing errors → autonomous organization), and infrastructure requirements are a function of the target level.
core_insights.why_it_matters: It gives a shared vocabulary for scoping infra investment: an L2 copilot does not need an event store, while an L4 operator that reads logs and fixes its own errors requires durable execution, observability, and a sandbox. It prevents over- or under-building.

evidence_quotes.text: Tool calling is a contract on tokens (JSON schemas).
Giving an LLM 20+ tools creates noise and wastes tokens when only 1 tool is needed.
Comparing the tool-calling approach with the code/language approach, highlighting why giving an LLM a massive menu of tools creates token waste and noise.

deep_dives.research_question: Holding model and task fixed, how do per-turn prompt tokens, total episode tokens, and task success scale with enumerated tool count (1, 5, 20, 50) versus an equivalent SDK-plus-code-execution interface — and at what tool count does the code interface's crossover point occur?
deep_dives.topic: Token economics of tool-schema surfaces vs. code interfaces
deep_dives.trigger_insight: collapses the per-turn token cost of tool schemas and removes the classifier/selection bottleneck
deep_dives.why: The talk asserts a large win from code interfaces but the mechanism is a fixed per-call schema tax plus a selection bottleneck. Without a measured crossover curve, teams cannot decide when migrating from a tool registry to an SDK is worth the sandbox, egress, and error-surface costs it introduces.

evidence_quotes.text: Agent step execution is decomposed into queue / worker / append-only event store
infrastructure and architecture required behind long-running AI agents

deep_dives.research_question: What fraction of agent steps replay identically when model outputs and external call results are memoized as events, and what is the minimum memoization set needed to reach step-level determinism without recording full network payloads?
deep_dives.topic: Replay determinism for event-sourced agent runs
deep_dives.trigger_insight: How is deterministic replay achieved when agent steps involve nondeterministic model sampling and external network calls?
deep_dives.why: Crash recovery and time-travel debugging are the payoff of moving the loop into a queue/worker/event store, but sampling and side-effecting external calls break naive replay. If replay diverges quickly, the audit-trail and debugging value is limited to log inspection rather than true re-execution.

evidence_quotes.text: Context grows every step, making re-sending the full context increasingly expensive.
Filesystem acts as the agent's extended context, reducing payload size in the context window.

deep_dives.research_question: Given steps N, context size per step, checkpoint interval, and re-read frequency, what checkpoint/spill policy minimizes total cost while keeping failure-recovery loss bounded, and how does the optimum shift between a 10-minute and a 6-hour run?
deep_dives.topic: Checkpoint and context-externalization granularity as a cost function of run length
deep_dives.trigger_insight: What is the right checkpoint and context-externalization granularity as a function of run length?
deep_dives.why: The claim that context cost grows every step is the economic failure mode that decides whether long runs are feasible at all. Without a parameterized model, 'spill to filesystem' and 'checkpoint often' are heuristics that can add I/O and re-read overhead faster than they save prompt tokens.

evidence_quotes.text: Network access must be strictly controlled with allowlisted domains and proxies for secrets.
Agents need a real working environment like a VM or Docker container.

deep_dives.research_question: How many real-world vendor SDKs and CLI clients authenticate successfully through a transparent secret-injecting proxy from inside a network-restricted sandbox without sandbox-specific shims, and where do they break?
deep_dives.topic: Credential-injecting egress proxy compatibility with unmodified third-party SDKs
deep_dives.trigger_insight: Prototype a transparent credential-injecting proxy and evaluate how many real SDKs work unmodified versus requiring sandbox-specific shims.
deep_dives.why: Pushing secrets out of the sandbox is only useful if general-purpose code still works inside it. Each SDK requiring a shim is a hidden integration tax and a silent runtime capability failure when an allowlisted domain is missing, so the breakage taxonomy determines whether the security boundary is deployable.

evidence_quotes.text: L4 is autonomous operators observing logs and fixing errors.
L5 is autonomous organization (acting like a CEO).
Understanding current agent autonomy levels helps engineers design the right infrastructure for the level of independence required.

deep_dives.research_question: Does each autonomy level require a distinct, minimally sufficient infrastructure set (sandbox, egress proxy, event store, observability), and do lower-level systems that skip a level's components exhibit the predicted failure modes under sustained load?
deep_dives.topic: Mapping the L0-L5 autonomy taxonomy onto concrete infrastructure requirements
deep_dives.trigger_insight: Construct a matrix of autonomy level vs. required components
deep_dives.why: The taxonomy is offered as an analogy, not a specification. If the level-to-component mapping is real, it becomes a scoping tool that prevents both over-building an L2 copilot and under-building an L4 operator that must read logs and repair itself.

key_claims.evidence: Filesystem acts as the agent's extended context, reducing payload size in the context window.
key_claims.verification_question: Compared to in-context accumulation, how much does file-based offload reduce total tokens and error rate on multi-hour tasks, accounting for re-read calls?

key_claims.claim: Long-running agent processes fail due to worker evictions, rollouts, and client disconnects.
key_claims.evidence: Processes die due to worker evictions, rollouts, or client disconnects.
key_claims.verification_question: What is the empirical distribution of failure causes and mean time between interruptions for agent runs of 1–8 hours in production?

key_claims.claim: Event sourcing over a queue/worker/event-store architecture enables crash recovery, time-travel debugging, audit trails, and deterministic replay.
key_claims.evidence: Event sourcing (queue, worker, event store) enables crash recovery, time-travel debugging, audit trails, and deterministic replay.
key_claims.verification_question: To what extent is replay actually deterministic when steps depend on model sampling and external services, and what is the recovery overhead from the last checkpoint?

key_claims.claim: Context cost grows every step because the full accumulated context is re-sent.
key_claims.evidence: Context grows every step, making re-sending the full context increasingly expensive.
key_claims.verification_question: How does total token spend scale with step count under naive context accumulation versus filesystem-externalized state?

key_claims.claim: Agents with code execution and proper harness infrastructure can complete multi-hour complex tasks without human intervention.
key_claims.evidence: Agents equipped with code execution and proper harness infrastructure can successfully complete multi-hour complex tasks without human intervention.
key_claims.verification_question: Was the 71-slide deck task completed end-to-end unattended, and what were the intervention count, failure rate, and total cost?

open_questions.question: How is deterministic replay achieved when agent steps involve nondeterministic model sampling and external network calls?
open_questions.research_direction: Prototype a replay harness that records model responses and external call results as events, then measure how often replay diverges and what must be memoized to reach step-level determinism.
open_questions.why_unresolved: The summary asserts that event sourcing enables deterministic replay and checkpoint resumption but gives no mechanism for handling nondeterministic step outputs or side-effecting external calls during replay.

open_questions.question: What is the right checkpoint and context-externalization granularity as a function of run length?
open_questions.research_direction: Build a cost model parameterized by steps, context size, checkpoint interval, and re-read frequency; validate against a measured multi-hour agent run.
open_questions.why_unresolved: The summary recommends queue-worker-eventstore for runs longer than a few minutes and filesystem offload in general, but provides no threshold analysis or cost model for checkpoint frequency.

open_questions.question: Do the reported token-reduction and accuracy gains from code execution over tool calling hold for non-coding, wide-action-space domains?
open_questions.research_direction: Run a controlled A/B on an identical task suite comparing tool-menu and SDK+code harnesses, measuring tokens, accuracy, and failure recovery separately.
open_questions.why_unresolved: The cited benchmarks (Vercel, Anthropic, Cloudflare, Microsoft) are reported without task characteristics or methodology in the summary, and the demonstrated case is a coding/presentation artifact task.

open_questions.question: Does the L0–L5 autonomy taxonomy map cleanly onto concrete infrastructure requirements?
open_questions.research_direction: Construct a matrix of autonomy level vs. required components (sandbox, egress proxy, event store, observability) and test whether lower-level systems that skip components exhibit the predicted failure modes.
open_questions.why_unresolved: The levels are offered as an analogy to self-driving cars, and the summary does not specify which infra components each level actually requires.

open_questions.question: How are secrets proxied for arbitrary third-party APIs without breaking general-purpose code in the sandbox?
open_questions.research_direction: Prototype a transparent credential-injecting proxy and evaluate how many real SDKs work unmodified versus requiring sandbox-specific shims.
open_questions.why_unresolved: Secret proxying is stated as a requirement, but no interface is described for how code inside the sandbox authenticates through the proxy.

project_ideas.based_on: Tool definitions are a fixed tax paid on every model call
project_ideas.hypothesis: For a fixed task suite, total episode tokens for a code-execution-plus-SDK harness are strictly lower than for an enumerated tool menu once the tool count exceeds a measurable crossover N*, with no loss in task success.
project_ideas.measurement: Tokens per successful task, success rate, and retry count as a function of tool count; report the crossover N* and the slope of schema-token growth per added tool.
project_ideas.name: Schema Tax Meter
project_ideas.poc: Build the same five-task suite twice against one model: once with an enumerated tool registry parameterized at 1/5/20/50 tools, once with a small primitive set (shell, read, write, edit) plus an SDK callable from Python; log per-turn prompt tokens, total tokens, success, and failure-recovery attempts.

project_ideas.based_on: Prototype a replay harness that records model responses and external call results as events
project_ideas.hypothesis: Recording model completions and external call results as events is sufficient to replay at least 95% of agent steps identically, and the residual divergence localizes to a small identifiable set of step types.
project_ideas.measurement: Percentage of steps replaying to identical state, per-step-type divergence rate, and recovery overhead measured as time from last checkpoint to resume.
project_ideas.name: Replay Divergence Recorder
project_ideas.poc: Instrument a durable agent loop that writes every step (prompt hash, model output, tool/shell invocation, network response) to an append-only log; implement a replay mode that serves recorded outputs from the log and flags any step whose post-execution state differs from the recorded state; run 20 multi-hour-style runs and rerun each log twice.

project_ideas.based_on: Proxying secrets keeps credentials out of the filesystem that the agent (and anything it downloads) can read
project_ideas.hypothesis: A transparent credential-injecting proxy with a domain allowlist lets the majority of common third-party SDKs run unmodified inside a sandbox, and the remaining failures cluster into a small number of predictable patterns.
project_ideas.measurement: Fraction of tested SDKs working unmodified versus requiring a shim, plus the per-failure-category counts and number of allowlist entries needed to reach that fraction.
project_ideas.name: Egress Conformance Suite
project_ideas.poc: Stand up a sandbox with no direct egress plus a proxy that injects secrets per allowlisted host; run a battery of real SDK clients (HTTP API clients, package managers, cloud CLIs) unmodified and catalogue each failure as missing allowlist entry, host-header/auth-header rewriting need, certificate trust issue, or non-HTTP transport.

project_ideas.based_on: Build a cost model parameterized by steps, context size, checkpoint interval, and re-read frequency
project_ideas.hypothesis: There exists an optimal checkpoint interval and spill policy for a given run length, and beyond a threshold run length the filesystem-externalized policy beats naive accumulation in total tokens net of re-read calls.
project_ideas.measurement: Total tokens and cost per completed run versus step count N for each policy; verified break-even step count where spilled state beats in-context accumulation including re-reads.
project_ideas.name: Context Spill Cost Model
project_ideas.poc: Instrument a long-horizon task with tunable parameters (checkpoint interval, artifact size threshold for spilling, re-read strategy) and measure actual token spend and success for naive accumulation versus spill-to-file policies across a sweep of run lengths from minutes to hours.

source.title: Search as Code: The Infrastructure Behind Long-Running Agents

summary.html:
Overview

  • Speaker: Aleksandr Nikolenko
  • Channel: PyData
  • Main topic: Infrastructure and architecture for long-running AI agents using Search-as-Code and durable infrastructure
  • Purpose: To explain how to build reliable, scalable infrastructure (sandboxes, event sourcing, delegation) for long-running AI agents that need to execute complex multi-step workflows over hours rather than milliseconds. Aleksandr Nikolenko, a member of the technical staff at Perplexity AI, discusses the infrastructure and architecture required behind long-running AI agents. He compares agent autonomy levels to self-driving cars (L0 to L5) and argues that code-based execution and a structured harness (SDK, Skills, Sandbox) are vastly superior to traditional tool-calling menus for complex, long-running agent tasks.

Topic Map

Levels of Agent Autonomy

  • Explanation: Drawing an analogy from self-driving cars, the speaker categorizes agent autonomy into levels ranging from manual execution (L0) to full autonomous organization (L5).
  • Key claims:
    • L0 is manual human execution.
    • L1 is text generation (Copilot).
    • L2 is Copilot with accept/decline loops.
    • L3 is delegated agents with goal-based loops.
    • L4 is autonomous operators observing logs and fixing errors.
    • L5 is autonomous organization (acting like a CEO).
  • Examples:
    • Cursor or Copilot for code suggestions.
    • Autonomous debugging and pull request deployment.
  • Terminology:
    • agent autonomy
    • driver assistance
    • copilot
    • delegated agent
    • autonomous operator
    • autonomous organization
  • Why it matters: Understanding current agent autonomy levels helps engineers design the right infrastructure for the level of independence required.

Vocabulary for an Agent: Tools vs. Language

  • Explanation: Comparing the tool-calling approach with the code/language approach, highlighting why giving an LLM a massive menu of tools creates token waste and noise.
  • Key claims:
    • Tool calling is a contract on tokens (JSON schemas).
    • Giving an LLM 20+ tools creates noise and wastes tokens when only 1 tool is needed.
    • Giving an LLM a language (like Python or bash) and an SDK is far more flexible and robust than a large menu of tools.
  • Examples:
    • Vercel, Anthropic, Cloudflare, and Microsoft benchmarks showing token reduction and accuracy improvements with tool search or code execution.
  • Terminology:
    • tool calling
    • JSON contract
    • token cost
    • SDK
    • Skill
    • Sandbox
  • Why it matters: Transitioning from tool menus to code-based interfaces drastically reduces token consumption and improves agent accuracy.

A Home for an Agent: The Sandbox

  • Explanation: Discussing the requirements for an agent's execution environment, including virtual machines, controlled network access, and filesystem persistence.
  • Key claims:
    • Agents need a real working environment like a VM or Docker container.
    • Filesystem acts as the agent's extended context, reducing payload size in the context window.
    • Network access must be strictly controlled with allowlisted domains and proxies for secrets.
  • Examples:
    • Codex CLI, Claude Code, and OpenCode CLI utilizing shell, read, write, and edit primitives.
  • Terminology:
    • sandbox
    • virtual machine
    • filesystem context
    • allowlisted domains
    • proxy secrets
  • Why it matters: Providing a secure, controlled sandbox allows agents to execute shell commands and write files safely without risking infrastructure.

An Agent That Works for Hours: Durable Infrastructure

  • Explanation: Addressing the challenges of long-running agent execution (context growth, durability, and control planes) using event sourcing.
  • Key claims:
    • Context grows every step, making re-sending the full context increasingly expensive.
    • Processes die due to worker evictions, rollouts, or client disconnects.
    • Event sourcing (queue, worker, event store) enables crash recovery, time-travel debugging, audit trails, and deterministic replay.
  • Examples:
    • Replaying an event log from a checkpoint when a worker crashes.
  • Terminology:
    • context growth
    • durability
    • control plane
    • event sourcing
    • event log
    • deterministic replay
    • checkpointing
  • Why it matters: Long-running agents require robust backend infrastructure to survive failures, manage context costs, and maintain auditability.

Key Points

Code is better than a menu of tools

  • Explanation: Giving models code execution primitives (Python/bash) instead of dozens of specific tool APIs reduces token usage and avoids classifier bottlenecks.
  • Evidence: Benchmarks from Vercel, Anthropic, Cloudflare, and Microsoft showing token reduction up to 99.9% and accuracy increases.
  • Practical implication: Build SDKs and skills in Python/bash rather than registering bloated tool definitions for every possible action.

The filesystem is the agent's context

  • Explanation: Instead of storing huge intermediate payloads in the LLM context window, write intermediate results to disk and reference file paths.
  • Evidence: Saves tokens and prevents context pollution with garbage data.
  • Practical implication: Instruct agents via AGENTS.md to write intermediate results to files and re-read on demand.

Event sourcing solves durability

  • Explanation: Treating agent execution steps as an append-only event log allows for resuming, replaying, time-travel debugging, and fault tolerance.
  • Evidence: Standard backend engineering patterns applied to AI agent loops.
  • Practical implication: Implement queue-worker-eventstore architectures for any agent run lasting longer than a few minutes.

Frameworks, Models & Processes

The Agent Harness (SDK, Skill, Sandbox)

  • How it works: Combines a model-execution loop with limited tool primitives in an isolated sandbox environment backed by a template.
  • Components:
    • Model + Loop
    • Limited tools (files, bash, python)
    • Isolated sandbox (file system, execution, outbound network)
    • Sandbox template
  • When to use: When building long-running, autonomous developer or research agents.

Decomposed Agent Architecture (Queue, Worker, Event Store)

  • How it works: Decouples task scheduling and step execution using an append-only event log for durability and replayability.
  • Components:
    • Queue (what to do next)
    • Worker (executes the step)
    • Event Store (append-only events)
  • When to use: For production agent systems that must survive worker crashes, deployments, and network drops.

Examples & Case Studies

Building a 71-slide presentation deck entirely via an autonomous agent using a filesystem, python scripts, and CLI commands.

  • Illustrates: The power of L4/L5 autonomous operators with file and shell access.
  • Lesson: Agents equipped with code execution and proper harness infrastructure can successfully complete multi-hour complex tasks without human intervention.

Actionable Takeaways

  • Immediate:
    • Replace large tool menus with code execution primitives (Python/bash).
    • Use filesystem persistence instead of bloated context windows.
    • Write clear agent instructions in markdown files (e.g., AGENTS.md).
  • Strategic:
    • View agent infrastructure through the lens of backend systems engineering (event sourcing, queues, sandboxes).
    • Design agent loops to outlive individual process lifetimes and client connections.
  • Questions to investigate:
    • How to optimize context compaction without losing critical reasoning history?
    • What are the cost trade-offs of running large numbers of sub-agents versus a single orchestrator?

summary.markdown:
## Overview
- **Speaker**: Aleksandr Nikolenko
- **Channel**: PyData
- **Main topic**: Infrastructure and architecture for long-running AI agents using Search-as-Code and durable infrastructure
- **Purpose**: To explain how to build reliable, scalable infrastructure (sandboxes, event sourcing, delegation) for long-running AI agents that need to execute complex multi-step workflows over hours rather than milliseconds.
Aleksandr Nikolenko, a member of the technical staff at Perplexity AI, discusses the infrastructure and architecture required behind long-running AI agents. He compares agent autonomy levels to self-driving cars (L0 to L5) and argues that code-based execution and a structured harness (SDK, Skills, Sandbox) are vastly superior to traditional tool-calling menus for complex, long-running agent tasks.
## Topic Map
### Levels of Agent Autonomy
- **Explanation**: Drawing an analogy from self-driving cars, the speaker categorizes agent autonomy into levels ranging from manual execution (L0) to full autonomous organization (L5).
- **Key claims**:
  - L0 is manual human execution.
  - L1 is text generation (Copilot).
  - L2 is Copilot with accept/decline loops.
  - L3 is delegated agents with goal-based loops.
  - L4 is autonomous operators observing logs and fixing errors.
  - L5 is autonomous organization (acting like a CEO).
- **Examples**:
  - Cursor or Copilot for code suggestions.
  - Autonomous debugging and pull request deployment.
- **Terminology**:
  - agent autonomy
  - driver assistance
  - copilot
  - delegated agent
  - autonomous operator
  - autonomous organization
- **Why it matters**: Understanding current agent autonomy levels helps engineers design the right infrastructure for the level of independence required.
### Vocabulary for an Agent: Tools vs. Language
- **Explanation**: Comparing the tool-calling approach with the code/language approach, highlighting why giving an LLM a massive menu of tools creates token waste and noise.
- **Key claims**:
  - Tool calling is a contract on tokens (JSON schemas).
  - Giving an LLM 20+ tools creates noise and wastes tokens when only 1 tool is needed.
  - Giving an LLM a language (like Python or bash) and an SDK is far more flexible and robust than a large menu of tools.
- **Examples**:
  - Vercel, Anthropic, Cloudflare, and Microsoft benchmarks showing token reduction and accuracy improvements with tool search or code execution.
- **Terminology**:
  - tool calling
  - JSON contract
  - token cost
  - SDK
  - Skill
  - Sandbox
- **Why it matters**: Transitioning from tool menus to code-based interfaces drastically reduces token consumption and improves agent accuracy.
### A Home for an Agent: The Sandbox
- **Explanation**: Discussing the requirements for an agent's execution environment, including virtual machines, controlled network access, and filesystem persistence.
- **Key claims**:
  - Agents need a real working environment like a VM or Docker container.
  - Filesystem acts as the agent's extended context, reducing payload size in the context window.
  - Network access must be strictly controlled with allowlisted domains and proxies for secrets.
- **Examples**:
  - Codex CLI, Claude Code, and OpenCode CLI utilizing shell, read, write, and edit primitives.
- **Terminology**:
  - sandbox
  - virtual machine
  - filesystem context
  - allowlisted domains
  - proxy secrets
- **Why it matters**: Providing a secure, controlled sandbox allows agents to execute shell commands and write files safely without risking infrastructure.
### An Agent That Works for Hours: Durable Infrastructure
- **Explanation**: Addressing the challenges of long-running agent execution (context growth, durability, and control planes) using event sourcing.
- **Key claims**:
  - Context grows every step, making re-sending the full context increasingly expensive.
  - Processes die due to worker evictions, rollouts, or client disconnects.
  - Event sourcing (queue, worker, event store) enables crash recovery, time-travel debugging, audit trails, and deterministic replay.
- **Examples**:
  - Replaying an event log from a checkpoint when a worker crashes.
- **Terminology**:
  - context growth
  - durability
  - control plane
  - event sourcing
  - event log
  - deterministic replay
  - checkpointing
- **Why it matters**: Long-running agents require robust backend infrastructure to survive failures, manage context costs, and maintain auditability.
## Key Points
### Code is better than a menu of tools
- **Explanation**: Giving models code execution primitives (Python/bash) instead of dozens of specific tool APIs reduces token usage and avoids classifier bottlenecks.
- **Evidence**: Benchmarks from Vercel, Anthropic, Cloudflare, and Microsoft showing token reduction up to 99.9% and accuracy increases.
- **Practical implication**: Build SDKs and skills in Python/bash rather than registering bloated tool definitions for every possible action.
### The filesystem is the agent's context
- **Explanation**: Instead of storing huge intermediate payloads in the LLM context window, write intermediate results to disk and reference file paths.
- **Evidence**: Saves tokens and prevents context pollution with garbage data.
- **Practical implication**: Instruct agents via AGENTS.md to write intermediate results to files and re-read on demand.
### Event sourcing solves durability
- **Explanation**: Treating agent execution steps as an append-only event log allows for resuming, replaying, time-travel debugging, and fault tolerance.
- **Evidence**: Standard backend engineering patterns applied to AI agent loops.
- **Practical implication**: Implement queue-worker-eventstore architectures for any agent run lasting longer than a few minutes.
## Frameworks, Models & Processes
### The Agent Harness (SDK, Skill, Sandbox)
- **How it works**: Combines a model-execution loop with limited tool primitives in an isolated sandbox environment backed by a template.
- **Components**:
  - Model + Loop
  - Limited tools (files, bash, python)
  - Isolated sandbox (file system, execution, outbound network)
  - Sandbox template
- **When to use**: When building long-running, autonomous developer or research agents.
### Decomposed Agent Architecture (Queue, Worker, Event Store)
- **How it works**: Decouples task scheduling and step execution using an append-only event log for durability and replayability.
- **Components**:
  - Queue (what to do next)
  - Worker (executes the step)
  - Event Store (append-only events)
- **When to use**: For production agent systems that must survive worker crashes, deployments, and network drops.
## Examples & Case Studies
### Building a 71-slide presentation deck entirely via an autonomous agent using a filesystem, python scripts, and CLI commands.
- **Illustrates**: The power of L4/L5 autonomous operators with file and shell access.
- **Lesson**: Agents equipped with code execution and proper harness infrastructure can successfully complete multi-hour complex tasks without human intervention.
## Actionable Takeaways
- **Immediate**:
  - Replace large tool menus with code execution primitives (Python/bash).
  - Use filesystem persistence instead of bloated context windows.
  - Write clear agent instructions in markdown files (e.g., AGENTS.md).
- **Strategic**:
  - View agent infrastructure through the lens of backend systems engineering (event sourcing, queues, sandboxes).
  - Design agent loops to outlive individual process lifetimes and client connections.
- **Questions to investigate**:
  - How to optimize context compaction without losing critical reasoning history?
  - What are the cost trade-offs of running large numbers of sub-agents versus a single orchestrator?
## Claims Worth Verifying
- Cloudflare achieved 99.9% input-token reduction using code execution instead of tool calling. (metric)
- Anthropic search tool discovery increased accuracy from 49% to 74%. (metric)
## Notable Quotes
> "Search as Code: Infrastructure behind long-running agents" (at 0:06)
> "The human D-X optimizes for discoverability; agent D-X for predictability."
> "The model lives in a VM — files, shell, browser, memory, tools — with one cable to the internet." (at 30:38)
> "A sandbox is useful because it is provisioned, not because it is empty." (at 32:05)
> "Cached garbage is still garbage." (at 45:49)
> "It's the best time to be an infrastructure engineer." (at 59:58)

- Sandboxes with filesystems act as externalized context to save tokens.
- Durable infrastructure using event sourcing enables crash recovery and replay for long-running agents.
